A block of mass m rests on a block of mass M on a smooth floor. A horizontal force F is applied to the upper block m. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is mu_s. Derive the largest F for which the blocks move together without slipping.

Builds on

  • A 5 kg block is already sliding to the right on a horizontal floor. A constant 18 N…

Conditions

  • The lower block has no other horizontal contact force from the floor.
  • The contact between the two blocks remains horizontal.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must rebuild the no-slip force account after the applied force moves to the other body, rather than copying the friction equation from the earlier stacked-block threshold item.

What stayed valid

The whole system still sets the shared acceleration, and the friction one block needs is still tested against μ_s N; what changes is which block needs the friction.

Answer

If the blocks move together, a=F/(m+M). The lower block needs friction f_required=Ma. With N=mg at the interface, no slip requires MF/(m+M) <= mu_s m g, so F_max = mu_s m g (m+M)/M.

  1. Under the no-slip assumption, treat both blocks as one system to obtain the common acceleration a=F/(m+M).
  2. Now isolate the lower block M. Its only horizontal force is the friction from the upper block, so f_required=Ma=MF/(m+M).
  3. The interface normal is N=mg because the upper block has no vertical acceleration or other vertical force.
  4. Static contact is feasible only while f_required <= mu_s N; equality gives the threshold F_max.

Rubric

  • Uses one common acceleration only under the provisional no-slip constraint.
  • Isolates the lower block to identify the required friction as Ma.
  • Compares the required friction with mu_s mg and solves the resulting threshold.

Independent check

The friction needed to accelerate the lower block is the quantity tested against the static limit; using f=mu_s N for every smaller F would erase the dependence on F.

Repair

Revisit: Assume no relative sliding provisionally and solve the tangential Newton-II equation for the static friction value f_required that would make that motion possible.

Lineage check

The whole system still sets the shared acceleration, and the friction one block needs is still tested against μ_s N; what changes is which block needs the friction.

The learner must rebuild the no-slip force account after the applied force moves to the other body, rather than copying the friction equation from the earlier stacked-block threshold item.

Two blocks A and B are initially touching on a smooth horizontal floor, with A to the left of B. A horizontal force F is suddenly applied to A toward the left, away from B. A proposed solution treats A+B as one connected system and writes a=F/(m_A+m_B). Decide whether that model is valid immediately after the force is applied. If it is not, state the two accelerations.

Builds on

  • Blocks A and B are side by side on a smooth horizontal floor, with A to the left of B…

Conditions

  • There is no glue, string, or other connector.
  • The contact is an ordinary normal interaction that cannot pull.
  • Take rightward as positive.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must decide that the common-acceleration connected-system model has ceased to apply, rather than being told that contact is maintained.

What stayed valid

A common acceleration still needs an active constraint, and a contact force still can only push; what changes is that the constraint has actually been lost.

Answer

The common-acceleration model is invalid because the force makes A separate from B and an ordinary normal contact cannot pull them together. Immediately after contact is lost, a_A=-F/m_A and a_B=0.

  1. The earlier common-acceleration rule applies only while an active condition fixes the blocks' separation.
  2. Here F drives A away from B, so maintaining contact would require a tensile contact force on B, which an ordinary normal interaction cannot supply.
  3. Once the contact force becomes zero, B has no horizontal force and therefore zero horizontal acceleration.
  4. A has the applied leftward force F, so with rightward positive its acceleration is -F/m_A.

Rubric

  • Rejects common acceleration because the stated contact cannot enforce fixed separation under the applied force.
  • Sets the post-separation contact force to zero.
  • Obtains a_A=-F/m_A and a_B=0 in the declared sign convention.

Independent check

The rejected value F/(m_A+m_B) would require B to accelerate left even though no horizontal interaction remains on B.

Repair

Revisit: Identify the connection/contact condition and state exactly which relative separation is fixed.

Lineage check

A common acceleration still needs an active constraint, and a contact force still can only push; what changes is that the constraint has actually been lost.

The learner must decide that the common-acceleration connected-system model has ceased to apply, rather than being told that contact is maintained.

A student claims that both T_A=T_B and a_A+a_B=0 must either survive together or fail together. Decide which statement can still be obtained from the bounded material, and which statement is no longer licensed.

Builds on

  • Masses m_A and m_B, with m_B > m_A, hang from the two ends of one taut massless…

Conditions

  • Coordinates y_A and y_B are measured positive away from the fixed pulley along the two straight string segments.
  • The string remains taut and inextensible and does not slip.
  • Do not invent a torque or rotational-inertia equation.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must preserve the kinematic length constraint while rejecting the equal-tension model after only the force-transmission assumption changes.

What stayed valid

The fixed string length still gives a_A + a_B = 0 in away-from-pulley coordinates; what changes is that the pulley is no longer ideal, so equal tension is no longer licensed.

Answer

The kinematic relation a_A+a_B=0 still follows from the fixed total string length. Equal tension T_A=T_B is no longer guaranteed by the taught ideal redirection model once appreciable pulley rotational inertia is introduced. A quantitative tension difference is outside this packet.

  1. The signed acceleration relation is derived from the inextensible string's fixed length and the two changing straight segments.
  2. That geometric argument does not use equality of tension magnitudes.
  3. The one-common-T rule was licensed by the ideal massless/frictionless redirection model.
  4. Introducing appreciable pulley rotational inertia breaks that force-transmission idealization, so the packet must refuse equal tension without supplying a replacement dynamics model.

Rubric

  • Retains a_A+a_B=0 from the fixed-length geometry.
  • Refuses to assert T_A=T_B after the ideal redirection assumption is broken.
  • Does not manufacture a numerical or symbolic nonideal-pulley tension relation.

Independent check

If the pulley is restored to the massless ideal model, both claims are licensed again, but for different reasons: geometry for the acceleration relation and force transmission for equal tension.

Repair

Revisit: Keep the kinematic string-length claim separate from the force-transmission claim: derive the acceleration relation from inextensibility and fixed geometry, and use equal tension only when the independent ideal-string/redirection assumptions license it.

Lineage check

The fixed string length still gives a_A + a_B = 0 in away-from-pulley coordinates; what changes is that the pulley is no longer ideal, so equal tension is no longer licensed.

The learner must preserve the kinematic length constraint while rejecting the equal-tension model after only the force-transmission assumption changes.

The same smooth fixed-incline problem is solved by two students. Student A uses axes parallel/perpendicular to the plane. Student B keeps horizontal/vertical laboratory axes. Decide whether both coordinate choices are physically valid, and explain why Student A's choice usually makes the contact constraint and acceleration easier to express.

Builds on

  • A block of mass m is released from rest on a smooth fixed plane inclined at angle…

Conditions

  • Both students use one consistent inertial frame.
  • The plane is fixed and smooth.
  • No numerical angle is required.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must translate the same fixed-incline dynamics between contact-aligned and laboratory axes without treating one representation as different physics.

What stayed valid

The forces, weight and normal reaction, and the block's physical acceleration down the slope stay the same; only the axes used to describe them change.

Answer

Both coordinate systems are valid if used consistently. Plane-aligned axes are usually simpler because maintained contact becomes a_perp=0 and the unknown acceleration has only a parallel component; horizontal/vertical axes require projecting both the normal force and the constrained acceleration.

  1. Changing axes does not change the physical forces or motion.
  2. In plane-aligned axes, the normal reaction lies on the perpendicular axis and the tangential motion lies on the parallel axis.
  3. The contact condition is therefore stated directly as a_perp=0.
  4. In horizontal/vertical axes the same normal and acceleration must be represented by components, which is valid but algebraically less direct.

Rubric

  • Accepts both coordinate systems as valid representations.
  • Identifies a_perp=0 as the simple contact statement in plane-aligned axes.
  • States that horizontal/vertical axes require extra projection rather than different physics.

Independent check

A correct solution in either coordinate system must predict the same physical acceleration vector and normal reaction.

Repair

Revisit: Choose axes that make the active constraint easy to express; for a fixed inclined contact, use parallel/perpendicular axes when helpful, resolve the physical forces into those axes, and write separate signed Newton-II equations.

Lineage check

The forces, weight and normal reaction, and the block's physical acceleration down the slope stay the same; only the axes used to describe them change.

The learner must translate the same fixed-incline dynamics between contact-aligned and laboratory axes without treating one representation as different physics.

A block is at rest on a rough incline. A controllable force P acts up the plane. In one trial P is slightly smaller than mg sin(theta); in another it is slightly larger than mg sin(theta), and in both trials the available static friction is sufficient to prevent motion. Determine the static-friction direction in each trial without assuming that friction always points uphill.

Builds on

  • A block rests on a rough fixed plane inclined at angle theta. The coefficient of…

Conditions

  • The plane is fixed.
  • The block remains at rest in both stated trials.
  • P acts exactly parallel to the plane.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must choose the static-friction direction from the changed slip tendency, including a zero-friction boundary, instead of carrying over the familiar downhill-gravity case.

What stayed valid

Friction still opposes the slip tendency the block would have without it; what changes is that a push along the slope can cancel that tendency or reverse it.

Answer

When P<mg sin(theta), the no-friction tendency is down the plane, so static friction acts up the plane. When P>mg sin(theta), the no-friction tendency is up the plane, so static friction acts down the plane. At P=mg sin(theta), the required static friction is zero.

  1. Friction direction follows the relative slip tendency that would exist without friction.
  2. Compare the applied uphill force P with the downhill gravity component mg sin(theta).
  3. If gravity's component is larger, friction must act uphill to maintain rest.
  4. If P is larger, friction must act downhill.
  5. If the two non-friction tangential forces balance exactly, no tangential friction is required.

Rubric

  • Uses the no-friction slip tendency rather than the object's current zero velocity.
  • Assigns uphill friction for P<mg sin(theta) and downhill friction for P>mg sin(theta).
  • Allows zero friction at P=mg sin(theta).

Independent check

The physical direction changes continuously through a zero-friction case rather than remaining permanently uphill.

Repair

Revisit: Imagine the relative sliding or tendency to slide if friction were absent, then point friction opposite that relative tendency.

Lineage check

Friction still opposes the slip tendency the block would have without it; what changes is that a push along the slope can cancel that tendency or reverse it.

The learner must choose the static-friction direction from the changed slip tendency, including a zero-friction boundary, instead of carrying over the familiar downhill-gravity case.

A block of mass m is held at rest on a rough fixed plane that rises to the right at angle theta. A horizontal force P pushes to the right. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Derive the condition on P and theta for the block to be able to remain at rest.

Builds on

  • A block of mass m is on a smooth fixed plane that rises to the right at angle theta…

Conditions

  • 0 < theta < 90 degrees.
  • The applied force is horizontal.
  • Do not assume the static-friction direction in advance; use a signed required value.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must integrate force decomposition, altered normal reaction, signed friction demand and static feasibility in dependency order rather than copying N=mg cos(theta) or f=mu_s N.

What stayed valid

The normal force from the perpendicular balance, the friction that rest requires, and the test against μ_s N all carry over; what changes is that a horizontal push alters both N and the required friction at once.

The deciding move

Use the sign of f_required to determine the required friction direction and test its magnitude against mu_s N.

Answer

With uphill positive, N=mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta). The static friction required by rest is f_required=mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta). Static equilibrium is feasible exactly when |mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta)| <= mu_s[mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta)].

  1. Resolve P into P cos(theta) uphill and P sin(theta) into the plane.
  2. The perpendicular rest condition gives N=mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta).
  3. The tangential rest equation P cos(theta)+f_s-mg sin(theta)=0 gives the signed required friction f_required=mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta).
  4. Do not choose a friction direction separately; the sign of f_required supplies it.
  5. The static model is feasible when the magnitude of that required value does not exceed mu_s N.

Rubric

  • Includes the inward perpendicular component P sin(theta) when finding N.
  • Solves a signed f_required from the tangential equilibrium equation.
  • Tests |f_required| against mu_s N instead of setting friction equal to its limit immediately.

Independent check

At P=0 the condition reduces to tan(theta)<=mu_s; if P cos(theta)=mg sin(theta), the required friction is zero.

Repair

Revisit: Build the chosen-body FBD and determine the normal reaction N from the force balance or acceleration perpendicular to the contact; do not assume N = mg.

Lineage check

The normal force from the perpendicular balance, the friction that rest requires, and the test against μ_s N all carry over; what changes is that a horizontal push alters both N and the required friction at once.

The learner must integrate force decomposition, altered normal reaction, signed friction demand and static feasibility in dependency order rather than copying N=mg cos(theta) or f=mu_s N.

A proposed plane-aligned solution writes the tangential force sum as mg + mg sin(theta) and the perpendicular force sum as N - mg - mg cos(theta). The solver says the component terms were added because the weight was resolved. Identify the modelling error and write the correct role of the weight in the two component equations.

Builds on

  • A block rests on a smooth fixed incline. A student draws three downward-related force…

Conditions

  • The block is on a smooth fixed incline.
  • Only gravity and the normal reaction act.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must recognize the same force/component double-counting error after it moves from a drawn FBD into algebraic component equations.

What stayed valid

Weight is still one force described by two components, and the normal force is still the only other interaction; what changes is that the double count appears in equations rather than on a drawing.

Answer

The solution double-counts the same weight vector. In plane-aligned equations, gravity contributes mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane; the unresolved mg is not added again. Thus the tangential gravity term is mg sin(theta), and the perpendicular equation uses N-mg cos(theta)=0 for maintained contact.

  1. Weight mg is one physical force, not three.
  2. Resolving it replaces its representation in the chosen component equations.
  3. The original vector magnitude mg is not itself a signed scalar component along either tilted axis.
  4. Use the two appropriate components in the two equations and keep the normal as the separate contact force.

Rubric

  • Identifies double-counting of gravity as the error.
  • Uses mg sin(theta) only in the tangential gravity contribution.
  • Uses mg cos(theta) only in the perpendicular gravity contribution and N separately.

Independent check

The corrected equations account for exactly two physical interactions: Earth-on-block gravity and plane-on-block normal contact.

Repair

Revisit: When a physical force is resolved into components for chosen axes, keep the body-force inventory unchanged: use the components as a representation of that one force in the equations, not as additional interaction forces alongside the original vector.

Lineage check

Weight is still one force described by two components, and the normal force is still the only other interaction; what changes is that the double count appears in equations rather than on a drawing.

The learner must recognize the same force/component double-counting error after it moves from a drawn FBD into algebraic component equations.

A block starts from rest and travels the same distance s down the same incline of angle theta in two trials. On a smooth surface the time is t_0. On a rough surface the block slides throughout and the time is t > t_0. Assuming kinetic friction coefficient mu_k is constant, derive mu_k in terms of theta, t_0 and t.

Builds on

  • A block is already sliding down a rough fixed plane inclined at angle theta. The…

Conditions

  • Both trials start from rest at the same point.
  • The incline angle and travel distance are unchanged.
  • The rough-surface trial has established downward sliding with constant mu_k.

Commit to a model or representation and your first relation before opening support.

Review and solution

What changed

The learner must combine the established rough-incline dynamics with an independent timing representation to infer the friction coefficient, rather than being asked directly for acceleration.

What stayed valid

The rough-slope acceleration g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ) and the smooth-slope g sin θ still hold; what changes is that μ_k must be inferred from travel times instead of being used to find an acceleration.

Answer

Smooth acceleration is a_0=g sin(theta), rough acceleration is a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)]. Since s=(1/2)at^2 from rest, a/a_0=t_0^2/t^2. Therefore mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2].

  1. The smooth trial gives a_0=g sin(theta).
  2. The rough sliding trial gives a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)].
  3. Equal distance from rest gives s=(1/2)a_0 t_0^2=(1/2)a t^2, hence a/a_0=t_0^2/t^2.
  4. Substitute the two incline accelerations and solve for mu_k.
  5. This yields mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2].

Rubric

  • Builds the smooth and rough incline accelerations from the corresponding force models.
  • Uses equal-distance constant-acceleration kinematics to relate a/a_0 to t_0^2/t^2.
  • Solves to mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2] and checks its limiting sign.

Independent check

Because t>t_0, the bracket is positive. If t approaches t_0, the inferred mu_k approaches zero.

Repair

Revisit: Use |f_s| = mu_s N only at impending slip; if relative sliding is already established, use |f_k| = mu_k N with direction opposing the relative sliding.

Lineage check

The rough-slope acceleration g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ) and the smooth-slope g sin θ still hold; what changes is that μ_k must be inferred from travel times instead of being used to find an acceleration.

The learner must combine the established rough-incline dynamics with an independent timing representation to infer the friction coefficient, rather than being asked directly for acceleration.
